notes.h: Dual-earner families and changing sex roles
notes.b: Reconciling paid work with family life depends on how a household divides its roles and tasks between its members.
points: A dual-earner family is one in which both partners are in paid employment.
A role is the set of behaviours and responsibilities expected of a person in a position such as parent, employee, partner or homemaker.
Traditional sex roles gave the man the main earning role and the woman the main responsibility for childcare and home care.
Sex roles have loosened as more women take up paid work and more men take an active part in childcare and housework.
Children learn sex roles from the way tasks are shared at home, as well as from school, peers and the media.
Role overload occurs when one person tries to perform several roles at the same time, for example employee, parent and homemaker, and cannot meet the demands of all of them.
Effects on the individual: less leisure and rest time, tiredness, and stress.
Effects on work: difficulty finding time for training, extra hours or promotion, and pressure to take work home.
Effects on the family: tension between partners and other family members, and neglect of family tasks that no one has time to do.
Vulnerable members, such as young children, an elderly relative or a family member who is ill, may have no one available to care for them.
Women often carry a larger share of the strain because they usually remain the main carers at home.
Role conflict arises when the expectations of one role clash with the expectations of another.
Example: a child becomes sick and needs a parent at home while a work deadline requires the parent to stay at work.
Priority choice: a parent must decide which role to put first at a given moment, and that decision often causes guilt.
Conflict between partners: one partner may not support the other's employment, or the couple may compete over career priorities.
Conflict with the employer: an employer may expect availability that clashes with school hours and childcare arrangements.
Outcome: family members may feel lonely or neglected, and the family may need outside help to resolve the conflict.

notes.h: Distribution of parental and home-care responsibilities
points: Parental responsibilities include feeding, supervising, transporting and supporting children, helping with homework, and giving emotional support.
Home-care responsibilities include cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, budgeting and maintaining the home.
Fair sharing: partners agree which tasks each one owns, so that tasks are not done only when one partner asks for help.
Labour-saving appliances, such as washing machines, dishwashers and microwave ovens, reduce the time needed for home-care tasks.
Outside help, such as paid childcare, cleaning services, or grandparents and other relatives, takes over some parental and home-care duties.
Older children can take on age-appropriate tasks, such as tidying their rooms or setting the table, which builds independence.
When both parents take an active part in care, children see shared parenting as normal, which models gender equality.

notes.h: Impact of dual-earner families on family life
points: Positive: a second income raises household living standards and reduces financial worry.
Positive: children may become more independent when they take on responsibilities.
Positive: when parents share tasks, children learn that care and housework are shared responsibilities.
Negative: less time for shared family activities and conversation can weaken family relationships.
Negative: children may feel lonely or neglected, especially at times such as after school or when they are ill.
Negative: extra responsibility falls on older children, who may become carers for younger siblings.
Negative: childcare costs can absorb a large part of the second income.

notes.h: Ways to reconcile employment with family responsibilities
notes.b: Employers and employees use working arrangements that give more control over when and where work is done.
points: Flexitime: the employee chooses start and finish times within agreed limits, so that the working day can fit around school hours.
Job-sharing: two employees share one full-time post, dividing the hours and responsibilities between them.
Parental leave: unpaid leave taken to care for a child, which may be taken in blocks or spread over an agreed period.
Career break: a temporary period of unpaid leave that allows the employee to return to the same job later.
Teleworking: working from home reduces commuting time and lets a parent be available around the home.
Part-time and term-time work: reduced hours allow the employee to be at home during school hours or school holidays.
Compressed working week: longer working days over fewer days free up time for family commitments.

notes.h: Investigation: survey of male and female roles in home tasks
points: Aim: to find out how male and female family members share twenty named home tasks.
Method step 1: list twenty home tasks, such as cooking, ironing, grocery shopping, car maintenance, paying bills and childminding.
Method step 2: design a questionnaire that asks who usually does each task: mainly male, mainly female, shared or someone else.
Method step 3: survey a sample of students, or their parents, and ask respondents to answer about their own household.
Method step 4: keep responses anonymous, so that no family or individual can be identified.
Analysis: count the answers in each category for each task and express each category as a percentage of the total answers.
Conclusion: the results show whether the sample's home tasks are still divided on traditional sex-role lines or are shared, and link this to dual-earner households.

keyTerms.definition: A family in which both partners are in paid employment.
The behaviours and responsibilities that a society or family expects of men and women.
The strain that results when one person tries to perform several roles at the same time and cannot meet all their demands.
The clash between the expectations of one role and the expectations of another role, such as work and parenthood.
The duties of caring for, supervising, supporting and guiding children.
The tasks of maintaining the home and feeding and clothing the family, such as cooking, cleaning and laundry.
A working arrangement in which employees choose their start and finish times within agreed limits.
An arrangement in which two people share one full-time job, splitting its hours and responsibilities.
Unpaid leave taken by a parent to care for a child.
A temporary period of unpaid leave from work that allows an employee to return to the same job later.
Doing paid work from home, using a computer and communication links rather than travelling to a workplace.

factCards.term: Three effects of role overload on family members
factCards.definition: 1. Reduced leisure and rest time. 2. Increased stress and tension between partners and family members. 3. Less time for each role, so work or family duties are neglected.

factCards.term: Four ways to share parental and home-care responsibilities
factCards.definition: 1. Agreeing a fair division of tasks between partners. 2. Using labour-saving appliances. 3. Getting outside help, such as paid childcare or relatives. 4. Giving older children age-appropriate jobs.

factCards.term: Four flexible working arrangements that help families
Two sources of conflict between partners in a dual-earner household
factCards.definition: 1. Disagreement over whose career takes priority. 2. One partner not supporting the other's paid work outside the home.

factCards.term: Three positive effects of dual-earner families on children
factCards.definition: 1. Children may become more independent. 2. Children learn that care and housework are shared. 3. Children see both parents actively involved in their upbringing.

factCards.term: First steps in the household task survey
factCards.definition: Choose twenty named home tasks, design a questionnaire asking who usually does each one, survey a sample anonymously, and count the answers in each category.

questions.prompt: Define role overload and state two effects it can have on a dual-earner family.
questions.model: Role overload: one person tries to perform several roles at the same time and cannot meet the demands of all of them. Effect 1: reduced leisure and rest time, leading to tiredness and stress. Effect 2: tension between partners and family members, or neglect of family tasks that no one has time to complete.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of dual-earner families on family life, with reference to role conflict and the distribution of parental and home-care responsibilities.
questions.model: Dual-earner family: both partners are in paid employment. Role conflict: the expectations of one role clash with another, for example a sick child needing a parent at home while a work deadline requires the parent to stay at work; a parent must choose a priority and may feel guilt; partners may compete over career priorities or one may not support the other's employment. Distribution of parental responsibilities: partners share supervision, transport, homework and emotional support; older children may take on extra duties; outside help such as paid childcare or relatives may take over some tasks. Distribution of home-care responsibilities: partners agree a fair division of cooking, cleaning and laundry; labour-saving appliances reduce the time needed. Positive impacts: higher household income and lower financial worry; children become more independent and learn that care is shared. Negative impacts: less time for shared family activities, weaker relationships, children feeling lonely or neglected, and childcare costs absorbing much of the second income. Reconciling strategies: flexitime, job-sharing, parental leave, career breaks and teleworking allow parents to fit work around family needs.
